messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 25
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 76

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Trauma-Related Events: Trauma-related events, Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Certain Songs: Certain songs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Happiness: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable., Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame, a twenty-five-year-old journalist, arrived at the clinic with a quiet, watchful posture that seemed to take up as little space as possible. He sat at the edge of the chair, his hands resting on his knees, dressed in a loose black hoodie despite the warm spring afternoon. He had come because his girlfriend, Maya, had finally convinced him that he could not keep going the way he was. For months he had been deteriorating, and she was afraid of what might happen if he did not talk to someone.

The event that changed everything had happened just over eight months ago. Kwame had been assigned to cover a peaceful protest downtown, one of many that summer. He had his press credentials around his neck and his camera in hand, moving through the crowd to get shots of the speeches. He remembered the sound of a song playing from a nearby car—something upbeat, he could not recall the name now without his stomach tightening—and then the sudden surge of police officers pushing into the crowd. He had tried to step back, to hold his press ID higher, but a baton caught him across the ribs and he went down. Another officer grabbed his camera and smashed it on the pavement. Kwame had curled up, shielding his head, and heard footsteps all around him, boots landing hard and fast. When it was over, he saw that a colleague, a young photographer named Amara, was not getting up. She had been hit in the head. She died later that night in the hospital.

In the weeks that followed, Kwame’s world shrank. He stopped going out after dark. He began wearing baggy, concealing clothing—hoodies, dark jackets, sunglasses even on cloudy days—because he had come to believe that standing out in any way made him a target. He was certain that if he looked nondescript enough, no one would notice him, no one would single him out. He avoided unfamiliar neighborhoods entirely, reasoning that he could not predict the dangers in a place he did not know. Every time he walked down a street, he found himself glancing over his shoulder, checking behind him, scanning for footsteps that might be closing in. He could not concentrate at work. Assignments that used to take him an hour now stretched into three because his mind would snag on a sound—a car door slamming, a raised voice—and he would lose the thread of his own thoughts. His editor noticed and pulled him from field assignments, telling him to focus on desk work. Kwame had always been a reporter who lived for the story; now he felt he was no longer capable of the work that had defined him.

His memory of that day was strange. When he tried to tell Maya what had happened, the words came out in fragments. He would start to describe the protest, then the song, then the boots, and then he would lose the thread entirely, unable to finish a single sentence. But the memory itself did not feel fragmented; it felt more real and vivid than ordinary memories. Sometimes, when he was alone in his apartment, he would hear the sound of the police officer’s radio crackling, or the music from that car, playing inside his head as clearly as if it were happening again. He could not stand silence because silence seemed to invite those sounds.

Kwame had once been a cheerful, energetic person who loved discovering new parts of the city and meeting strangers. Now he described himself as miserable, certain that his life had been destroyed. He avoided anything that reminded him of Amara—her name in an email, a photograph of the two of them at a previous protest, a news story about police accountability. He also avoided feeling anything at all, positive or negative, because emotions felt dangerous. He kept himself flat, neutral, unresponsive. Maya told him she missed the man she had fallen in love with. He knew she was right, but he did not know how to find him again.

What finally brought Kwame to the clinic was a moment of panic in a grocery store. A customer behind him dropped a jar, and the sharp sound of glass hitting the floor sent Kwame ducking and shaking. He fled the store without buying anything. Later that night, Maya held his hand and said he could not live like this anymore. He agreed, because he was terrified that if he did not change, he would lose her, and he would lose himself for good. He hoped, more than anything, that someone could help him feel safe in his own skin again. But he was also afraid that the man he used to be—the journalist who walked into any crowd without hesitation—was gone forever, and that no amount of therapy would bring him back.
